lesson.title: Big-O Notation: A Language for Describing Growth
lesson.summary: Big-O notation gives programmers a common language for describing how the running time or memory needs of an algorithm grow as the size of its input grows, so that different approaches to the same problem can be compared fairly.
lesson.body:
Once you can design an algorithm to solve a problem (the skill you built in Algorithm Design), a new question appears immediately: is this a good algorithm? Two different algorithms can both produce the correct answer, but one might finish in a blink while the other grinds to a halt on a large input. Big-O notation is the tool computer scientists use to answer that question in a precise, comparable way.

The key idea behind Big-O is that we do not care about how fast any single computer runs code today. A faster laptop, a better compiler, or a language written in C instead of Python will change the actual number of seconds a program takes, but none of that tells you anything fundamental about the algorithm itself. What we want instead is a description of how the amount of work grows as the input size, usually called n, grows. Big-O captures that growth rate while ignoring constant factors, like being twice as fast on one machine, and lower-order terms, details that stop mattering once n gets large.

Consider this simple search function.

def contains(values, target):
    for v in values:
        if v == target:
            return True
    return False

In the worst case, this loop looks at every one of the n elements once, so we say this algorithm runs in O(n) time. If we doubled the length of values, we would expect roughly twice as many comparisons in the worst case. Now compare it to this function.

def first_element(values):
    return values[0]

This function does the same fixed amount of work no matter how long values is. Whether it has 10 items or 10 million, it does one lookup. We say this runs in O(1) time.

Formally, we say a function f(n) is O(g(n)) if, for large enough n, f(n) grows no faster than some constant multiple of g(n). In practice, you rarely need the formal definition to use Big-O well. What matters is the habit: strip away constants, so a loop that runs 3n + 5 times becomes O(n), and strip away lower-order terms, so an algorithm that does n^2 + n comparisons becomes O(n^2), because n^2 dominates once n is large. Big-O describes the shape of growth, not the exact count.

By convention, Big-O describes the worst case, the slowest an algorithm could possibly run for an input of size n, unless we explicitly say we mean best case or average case, a distinction covered later in this unit under Best, Average, and Worst Case. This convention exists because worst case gives a guarantee: no matter what input you hand the algorithm, it will not perform worse than its Big-O bound suggests. That guarantee is exactly what you need when you cannot control or predict what data a real program will see.

This chapter's job was to introduce Big-O as a language. The chapters that follow give you the vocabulary of that language, the specific growth rates like O(1), O(n), O(n^2), O(log n), and O(n log n) that show up constantly in real programs, plus the counting techniques and testing habits that let you determine which one applies to a piece of code you write or read.
